reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: A deviated septum is a displacement of the bony or cartilaginous nasal septum from the midline and is extremely common, often asymptomatic
It may be developmental (from differential growth of the septum and palate) or acquired following nasal trauma, sometimes at birth
The dominant symptom is nasal obstruction, which may be unilateral or, with an S-shaped deviation, affect both sides
Deviations take various forms including a spur, a C- or S-shaped bend, or dislocation of the caudal septum into the vestibule
A prominent spur can press on the lateral wall and trigger headache or referred facial pain, and can contribute to recurrent epistaxis over the exposed area
Septal deviation predisposes to sinus drainage problems and recurrent sinusitis and can worsen snoring and obstructive symptoms
Diagnosis rests on anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy, decongesting the mucosa to distinguish a structural deviation from turbinate hypertrophy
Symptomatic deviation is corrected surgically by septoplasty (or submucous resection), often with turbinate reduction, while asymptomatic deviation needs no treatment
reference.pathophysiology: The nasal septum is formed by the septal cartilage, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and the vomer, meeting the maxillary and palatine crests. Deviation arises when these components grow at differing rates or are displaced by trauma, so the septum buckles or angulates away from the midline. The deviation narrows the airway on the concave side and may obstruct the osteomeatal complex, impairing sinus ventilation and mucociliary drainage. Compensatory hypertrophy of the turbinate on the wider side can paradoxically cause obstruction there as well. Mucosa stretched over a spur becomes dry and prone to bleeding, and contact between the deviated septum and the lateral nasal wall can generate pressure-referred headache.
additionalDifferentials: Allergic or non-allergic rhinitis with mucosal congestion
Intranasal mass or tumour causing unilateral obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Anterior rhinoscopy after decongestion to assess the septum and turbinates
Nasal endoscopy for a full view of the posterior septum and osteomeatal complex
CT of the paranasal sinuses when sinus disease or surgery is planned
Assessment of nasal airflow and, where indicated, allergy testing to identify a mucosal component
Photographic and functional assessment if external nasal deformity coexists
redFlags: Strictly unilateral obstruction with blood-stained discharge suggesting a tumour rather than simple deviation
A septal swelling after trauma suggesting a septal haematoma or abscess needing urgent drainage
Progressive external deformity, crusting or perforation raising concern for granulomatous or destructive disease
Persistent facial pain or visual symptoms suggesting significant sinus complication
reference.prognosis: Septoplasty relieves obstruction and associated symptoms in most patients with good long-term results, though some residual deviation or persistent turbinate-related congestion may remain; untreated symptomatic deviation can perpetuate sinus problems and sleep-disordered breathing.
pitfalls: Attributing all nasal obstruction to the septum while overlooking turbinate hypertrophy, polyps or allergy
Operating on an asymptomatic deviation found incidentally
Missing a septal haematoma after trauma, risking cartilage necrosis and saddle deformity
Failing to examine after decongestion, which distinguishes structural from mucosal obstruction
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
